I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. At 66, my back isn't what it was, but I know this soil. My sons have moved to the city, so I work the fields mostly alone with a bit of help during harvest. I have about 7 mu under cultivation.

Here in the North China Plain, there's really only one system that makes sense: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. I've done this rotation for forty years. It uses the land fully, the maize stubble helps the soil a little, and I know the markets for both crops. I'm not going to try cotton or vegetables — those need more labor and attention than I can manage alone now.

For wheat, I'll use an improved variety — Jimai 22 or whatever the seed shop in town is selling that's done well locally. I've used traditional seeds before, but the improved ones yield better and resist lodging. I'll plough with a rotary tiller after maize harvest in October, apply base fertilizer, then seed. I'll irrigate before winter sets in, then again at jointing and heading. Maybe a fourth time if the spring is dry. I'll spray for weeds in late autumn and watch for rust in spring.

For maize, I direct-seed right after wheat harvest in June — no time to plough, the window is tight. I'll use a hybrid, probably Zhengdan 958 or similar. One topdressing of urea at the knee-high stage. One or two irrigations if July is dry. I don't spray much on maize unless I see corn borer damage.

I won't push yields beyond what this soil and my water quota allow. Groundwater here is already deep.
